claim: Over 800 proteins were identified across polysome gradient fractions in yeast cells.
source: Over 800 proteins were identified across polysome gradient fractions, including ribosomal proteins, translation factors, and many others without previously described translation-related roles, including numerous metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of proteins identified in their mass spectrometry analysis of polysome fractions.

claim: Polysome profiling combined with mass spectrometry identified ribosomal proteins, translation factors, and metabolic enzymes associated with translating ribosomes.
source: Over 800 proteins were identified across polysome gradient fractions, including ribosomal proteins, translation factors, and many others without previously described translation-related roles, including numerous metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the types of proteins identified in their experimental approach.

claim: Variations in patterns of polysome enrichment were identified in both unstressed and stressed cells.
source: We identified variations in patterns of PE in both unstressed and stressed cells and identified proteins enriched in heavy polysomes during stress.
evidence: The manuscript reports observing variations in polysome enrichment patterns across different conditions.

claim: Proteins enriched in heavy polysomes during stress were identified.
source: We identified variations in patterns of PE in both unstressed and stressed cells and identified proteins enriched in heavy polysomes during stress.
evidence: The manuscript reports identifying specific proteins that remain associated with heavy polysomes during stress conditions.

claim: Deletion of AAT2 conferred growth sensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: Genetic screening of polysome-enriched RBPs identified the cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase, Aat2, as a ribosome-associated protein whose deletion conferred growth sensitivity to oxidative stress.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from genetic screening showing that aat2Δ cells are sensitive to oxidative stress.

claim: Loss of Aat2 caused aberrantly high activation of the ISR via enhanced eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Loss of Aat2 caused aberrantly high activation of the ISR via enhanced eIF2α phosphorylation and GCN4 activation.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing increased eIF2α phosphorylation in aat2Δ cells.

claim: Loss of Aat2 caused GCN4 activation.
source: Loss of Aat2 caused aberrantly high activation of the ISR via enhanced eIF2α phosphorylation and GCN4 activation.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing increased GCN4 activation in aat2Δ cells.

claim: Non-catalytic AAT2 mutants retained polysome association.
source: Importantly, non-catalytic AAT2 mutants retained polysome association and did not show heightened stress sensitivity.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing that catalytically inactive Aat2 mutants still bind to polysomes.

claim: Non-catalytic AAT2 mutants did not show heightened stress sensitivity.
source: Importantly, non-catalytic AAT2 mutants retained polysome association and did not show heightened stress sensitivity.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing that catalytically inactive Aat2 mutants do not exhibit the stress sensitivity phenotype of aat2Δ cells.

claim: Aat2 has a ribosome-associated translational regulatory function that modulates the ISR independent of its aspartate aminotransferase activity.
source: Aat2 therefore has a separate ribosome-associated translational regulatory or 'moonlighting' function that modulates the ISR independent of its aspartate aminotransferase activity.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on data showing that catalytically inactive mutants retain ribosome binding and do not show stress sensitivity.

claim: Translation and its regulation require the concerted action of translation factors, tRNAs, ribosomes, and RNA-binding proteins.
source: Translation and its regulation are highly complex processes requiring the concerted action of numerous factors associated with mRNAs: translation factors (TFs), tRNAs, ribosomes, and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) (Dever et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dever et al., 2016.

claim: The translation apparatus can immediately impact protein content of cells to meet changing conditions.
source: Importantly, the translation apparatus is nimble in that its regulation immediately impacts upon the protein content of cells to meet changing conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about translation regulation supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The integrated stress response is common to all eukaryotes.
source: One translational control pathway common to all eukaryotes is called the integrated stress response (ISR) (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016) also known as general amino acid control in yeast.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016.

claim: The integrated stress response is also known as general amino acid control in yeast.
source: One translational control pathway common to all eukaryotes is called the integrated stress response (ISR) (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016) also known as general amino acid control in yeast.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field.

claim: Distinct cellular stress signals activate one or more of a family of protein kinases (GCN2, PKR, PERK, and HRI) that phosphorylate eIF2 on a conserved serine residue of its alpha subunit.
source: Distinct cellular stress signals activate one or more of a family of protein kinases (GCN2, PKR, PERK, and HRI) that each phosphorylate the general translation initiation factor eIF2 on a conserved single serine residue of its alpha subunit (Wek, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wek, 2018.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2 causes a rapid global downregulation of protein synthesis.
source: This causes a rapid global downregulation of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a well-established consequence of eIF2 phosphorylation in the ISR.

claim: Under active translation conditions, eIF2 in its GTP-bound form recruits initiator tRNA to ribosomes.
source: Under active translation conditions, eIF2 in its GTP-bound form recruits initiator tRNA to ribosomes.
evidence: This is a fundamental mechanism of translation initiation.

claim: Phosphorylated eIF2 forms an inhibited complex with eIF2B.
source: Phosphorylated eIF2 instead forms an inhibited complex with the key guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B, which otherwise generates active eIF2-GTP (Pavitt, 2018; Adomavicius et al., 2019; Kashiwagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pavitt, 2018; Adomavicius et al., 2019; Kashiwagi et al., 2019.

claim: eIF2B generates active eIF2-GTP.
source: Phosphorylated eIF2 instead forms an inhibited complex with the key guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B, which otherwise generates active eIF2-GTP (Pavitt, 2018; Adomavicius et al., 2019; Kashiwagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pavitt, 2018; Adomavicius et al., 2019; Kashiwagi et al., 2019.

claim: Not all translation is inhibited by the ISR.
source: However, not all translation is inhibited by the ISR.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of the ISR where certain mRNAs continue to be translated.

claim: mRNAs encoding stress-protective proteins need to be translated for cells to adapt to altered cellular environment.
source: mRNAs encoding stress-protective proteins need to be translated for cells to adapt to the altered cellular environment.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for stress adaptation.

claim: The 5′ UTRs of some translationally controlled mRNAs contain cis-acting elements promoting their translation when bulk protein synthesis is attenuated.
source: The 5′ untranslated regions (5′UTRs) of some translationally controlled mRNAs contain cis-acting elements promoting their translation when bulk protein synthesis is attenuated (Hinnebusch et al., 2016; Wek, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hinnebusch et al., 2016; Wek, 2018.

claim: ATF4 and GCN4 mRNAs are transcriptional activators whose expression is controlled via regulated ribosome reinitiation at upstream open reading frames.
source: Key examples include the mammalian ATF4 and yeast GCN4 mRNAs, which are both transcriptional activators whose expression is controlled via regulated ribosome reinitiation at upstream open reading frames (uORFs) (Hinnebusch et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hinnebusch et al., 2016.

claim: Once stress has been neutralised, translation patterns revert to steady state, restoring proteostasis.
source: Once the stress has been neutralised, translation patterns revert to steady state, restoring proteostasis (Crawford and Pavitt, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Crawford and Pavitt, 2019.

claim: In the ISR, restoration of proteostasis requires the dephosphorylation of eIF2.
source: In the ISR, this requires the dephosphorylation of eIF2 (Wek, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wek, 2018.

claim: In humans, failure to restore proteostasis in a timely manner can contribute to cognitive disorders and cancer.
source: In humans a failure to restore proteostasis in a timely manner can contribute to a range of diseases, including cognitive disorders and cancer (Costa-Mattioli and Walter, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Costa-Mattioli and Walter, 2020.

claim: Inhibiting RNA helicases that promote ribosome recruitment and unwinding of secondary structures during 5′UTR scanning reduces translation significantly.
source: Inhibiting RNA helicases that promote ribosome recruitment and the unwinding of secondary structures during 5′UTR scanning has been shown to reduce translation significantly (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sen et al., 2015.

claim: In yeast, both glucose starvation and heat shock stresses are accompanied by a dramatic reduction in mRNA binding by eIF4A and Ded1 RNA helicases.
source: In yeast, both glucose starvation and heat shock stresses are accompanied by a dramatic reduction in mRNA binding by both the eIF4A and Ded1 RNA helicases (Castelli et al., 2011; Bresson et al., 2020), which contributes to very rapid translational repression, within 1 min following glucose withdrawal (Ashe et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Castelli et al., 2011; Bresson et al., 2020; Ashe et al., 2000.

claim: Reduction in mRNA binding by eIF4A and Ded1 contributes to very rapid translational repression within 1 min following glucose withdrawal.
source: In yeast, both glucose starvation and heat shock stresses are accompanied by a dramatic reduction in mRNA binding by both the eIF4A and Ded1 RNA helicases (Castelli et al., 2011; Bresson et al., 2020), which contributes to very rapid translational repression, within 1 min following glucose withdrawal (Ashe et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ashe et al., 2000.

claim: Translation elongation can be regulated through modulation of the activity of elongation factors such as eEF2.
source: In addition, translation elongation can be regulated through modulation of the activity of elongation factors such as eEF2, which is modified downstream of some stress signalling pathways, including oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a general statement about elongation regulation.

claim: eEF2 is modified downstream of some stress signalling pathways, including oxidative stress.
source: In addition, translation elongation can be regulated through modulation of the activity of elongation factors such as eEF2, which is modified downstream of some stress signalling pathways, including oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a general statement about eEF2 modification during stress.

claim: tRNA availability controls elongation rates.
source: tRNA availability also controls elongation rates.
evidence: This is an established mechanism of elongation control.

claim: Local variations in codon usage and ribosomal pausing and stalling events slow elongation.
source: Local variations in codon usage and ribosomal pausing and stalling events all slow elongation (Dever and Green, 2012; Schuller et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dever and Green, 2012; Schuller et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019; Tesina et al., 2020.

claim: Stalled ribosomes lead to ribosome collisions, which can activate Gcn2 and the ISR.
source: Stalled ribosomes lead to ribosome collisions, which can activate Gcn2 and the ISR (Wu et al., 2020; Pochopien et al., 2021; Yan and Zaher, 2021) as well as ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathways that recycle stalled ribosomes and degrade defective mRNAs (D'Orazio and Green, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2020; Pochopien et al., 2021; Yan and Zaher, 2021.

claim: Stalled ribosomes activate ribosome-associated quality control pathways that recycle stalled ribosomes and degrade defective mRNAs.
source: Stalled ribosomes lead to ribosome collisions, which can activate Gcn2 and the ISR (Wu et al., 2020; Pochopien et al., 2021; Yan and Zaher, 2021) as well as ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathways that recycle stalled ribosomes and degrade defective mRNAs (D'Orazio and Green, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to D'Orazio and Green, 2021.

claim: Ribosomes are not necessarily uniform and can vary between conditions and cell types.
source: Ribosomes themselves are not necessarily uniform and can vary between conditions and cell types (Slavov et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Slavov et al., 2015.

claim: Variation in ribosome composition can confer preferences for binding to different subsets of mRNAs.
source: Variation in ribosome composition can confer preferences for binding to different subsets of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a general statement about ribosome heterogeneity.

claim: High salt and raised pH reduce Rps26/eS26 incorporation into yeast ribosomes.
source: Examples include the ribosomal protein (RP) Rps26/eS26, where both high salt and raised pH reduce its incorporation into yeast ribosomes.
evidence: This is a specific example of ribosome heterogeneity.

claim: Rps26-deficient ribosomes are proposed to preferentially translate stress-responsive mRNAs via altered Kozak sequence recognition preferences.
source: Rps26-deficient ribosomes are proposed to preferentially translate stress-responsive mRNAs via altered Kozak sequence recognition preferences (Ferretti et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ferretti et al., 2017.

claim: Some paralogous ribosomal proteins have specific roles in translational regulation.
source: Furthermore, some paralogous RPs, where two genes encode the same RP, have been demonstrated to have specific roles in translational regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about RP paralogs.

claim: Yeast Rpl1a/uL1 and Rpl1b show preferences for translating different sets of mRNAs.
source: For example, yeast Rpl1a/uL1 and Rpl1b show preferences for translating different sets of mRNAs, as Rpl1b-containing ribosomes promote more efficient translation of mitochondrial proteins required for respiratory growth (Segev and Gerst, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Segev and Gerst, 2018.

claim: Rpl1b-containing ribosomes promote more efficient translation of mitochondrial proteins required for respiratory growth.
source: For example, yeast Rpl1a/uL1 and Rpl1b show preferences for translating different sets of mRNAs, as Rpl1b-containing ribosomes promote more efficient translation of mitochondrial proteins required for respiratory growth (Segev and Gerst, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Segev and Gerst, 2018.

claim: Mutations in ribosomal proteins lead to Diamond–Blackfan Anemia and other ribosomopathies in humans.
source: Mutations in RPs lead to Diamond–Blackfan Anemia and other ribosomopathies in humans, which might imply specialised roles for RP-deficient or paralog-specific ribosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosomopathies.

claim: Reducing the abundance of active ribosomes via defects in ribosomal proteins likely changes the balance of expression of mRNAs observed in different cells or tissues, potentially contributing to ribosomopathies.
source: Alternatively, reducing the abundance of active ribosomes via defects in RPs likely changes the balance of expression of mRNAs observed in different cells or tissues, potentially contributing to ribosomopathies (Mills and Green, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mills and Green, 2017.

claim: RBPs and ribosome-interacting proteins contribute to translational control.
source: RBPs and ribosome-interacting proteins also contribute to translational control.
evidence: This is a general statement about RBP function.

claim: Several RBPs have been observed to modulate the expression of sets of target mRNAs, which range from a few target transcripts to several thousand.
source: Several RBPs have been observed to modulate the expression of sets of target mRNAs, which range from a few target transcripts to several thousand (Hogan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hogan et al., 2008.

claim: The RBP CPEB is only recruited to mRNAs containing a cytoplasmic polyadenylation element and helps to modulate ribosome recruitment and translation.
source: For example, the RBP CPEB is only recruited to mRNAs containing a cytoplasmic polyadenylation element and helps to modulate ribosome recruitment and translation (Richter, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Richter, 2007.

claim: Multiple studies have attempted to identify mRNA targets of specific RBPs or identify new RBPs across a range of organisms.
source: Multiple studies have attempted to either identify mRNA targets of specific RBPs (Hogan et al., 2008) or identify new RBPs across a range of organisms, using a variety of methods (Hentze et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hogan et al., 2008 and Hentze et al., 2018.

claim: Studies have uncovered an unexpectedly large number of metabolic enzymes that bind RNA.
source: Curiously, these latter studies have uncovered an unexpectedly large number of metabolic enzymes that bind RNA.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from RBP identification studies.

claim: Very few newly recognised RBPs have a defined role in RNA biology.
source: Very few of these newly recognised RBPs have a defined role in RNA biology, but it has been suggested that many could have a second 'moonlighting' function when bound to RNA.
evidence: This is a summary of the state of knowledge about newly identified RBPs.

claim: Many newly recognised RBPs could have a second 'moonlighting' function when bound to RNA.
source: Very few of these newly recognised RBPs have a defined role in RNA biology, but it has been suggested that many could have a second 'moonlighting' function when bound to RNA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functions of newly identified RBPs.

claim: Undiscovered post-transcriptional regulatory networks may link gene expression and intermediary metabolism.
source: These results highlight the possibility that undiscovered post-transcriptional regulatory networks link gene expression and intermediary metabolism (Hentze and Preiss, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hentze and Preiss, 2010.

claim: A complex interplay exists between mRNA-specific elements, RBPs, and ribosome-associated factors that may enable selected stress-responsive mRNAs to escape globally repressive regulatory mechanisms.
source: A model has therefore emerged of a complex interplay between mRNA-specific elements, RBPs, and ribosome-associated factors that may combine to enable selected stress-responsive mRNAs to escape globally repressive regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary of current models in the field.

claim: Oxidative stress caused by H2O2 brings about rapid translational repression via Gcn2 activation and the ISR.
source: Oxidative stress caused by the addition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) brings about rapid translational repression via Gcn2 activation and the ISR (Shenton et al., 2006), as well as the induction of antioxidant enzymes at both the transcriptional and translational levels to ameliorate the stress (Morano et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shenton et al., 2006 and Morano et al., 2012.

claim: Oxidative stress induces antioxidant enzymes at both the transcriptional and translational levels to ameliorate the stress.
source: Oxidative stress caused by the addition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) brings about rapid translational repression via Gcn2 activation and the ISR (Shenton et al., 2006), as well as the induction of antioxidant enzymes at both the transcriptional and translational levels to ameliorate the stress (Morano et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morano et al., 2012.

claim: How antioxidant enzymes are translated under repressive conditions during oxidative stress is unclear.
source: How these antioxidant enzymes are translated under such repressive conditions is unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: 3-AT is a well-characterised inhibitor of histidine biosynthesis.
source: In parallel, we assessed how cells respond to amino acid starvation caused by the addition of 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT), a well-characterised inhibitor of histidine biosynthesis (Hinnebusch, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hinnebusch, 2005.

claim: Both H2O2 and 3-AT activate the yeast ISR and translation of GCN4.
source: Both stresses activate the yeast ISR and translation of GCN4 (Hinnebusch; Shenton et al., 2006) but also need to promote the expression of different stress-specific genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hinnebusch and Shenton et al., 2006.

claim: H2O2 and 3-AT need to promote the expression of different stress-specific genes.
source: Both stresses activate the yeast ISR and translation of GCN4 (Hinnebusch; Shenton et al., 2006) but also need to promote the expression of different stress-specific genes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about stress-specific responses.

claim: The changes in polysome enrichment of proteins in response to H2O2 and 3-AT are remarkably well correlated.
source: We find that the changes in polysome enrichment (PE) of proteins in response to both stresses are remarkably well correlated, with similar changes observed across both stresses for TFs, RPs, and a wide range of RBPs including metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their data analysis.

claim: Similar changes in polysome enrichment were observed across both stresses for translation factors, ribosomal proteins, and a wide range of RBPs including metabolic enzymes.
source: We find that the changes in polysome enrichment (PE) of proteins in response to both stresses are remarkably well correlated, with similar changes observed across both stresses for TFs, RPs, and a wide range of RBPs including metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their data analysis.

claim: Some RBPs closely followed the polysome enrichment profiles of ribosomal proteins during stress by accumulating in the 80S/monosomal fraction.
source: While some RBPs closely followed the PE profiles of RPs during stress by accumulating in the 80S/monosomal fraction, other proteins maintained or enhanced their association with the remaining heavy polysomes during the stress response.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their data analysis.

claim: Some proteins maintained or enhanced their association with heavy polysomes during the stress response.
source: While some RBPs closely followed the PE profiles of RPs during stress by accumulating in the 80S/monosomal fraction, other proteins maintained or enhanced their association with the remaining heavy polysomes during the stress response.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their data analysis.

claim: Aat2 is a novel ribosome-interacting protein with a 'moonlighting' function.
source: By screening candidate RBP knockout strains for oxidative stress phenotypes, we identified cytoplasmic aspartate amino transferase (Aat2) as a novel ribosome-interacting protein with a 'moonlighting' function.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a conclusion from their screening and characterization experiments.

claim: Aat2 binds to 60S ribosomes.
source: We show that Aat2 binds to 60S ribosomes and moderates Gcn2 activation in response to H2O2.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their experiments.

claim: Aat2 moderates Gcn2 activation in response to H2O2.
source: We show that Aat2 binds to 60S ribosomes and moderates Gcn2 activation in response to H2O2.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a finding from their experiments.

claim: The stress-response role of Aat2 is independent of its metabolic role.
source: Remarkably, mutational analyses show that the stress-response role is independent of its metabolic role.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a conclusion from their mutational analysis.

claim: 0.45 mM H2O2 treatment for 15 min caused an interruption to cell growth.
source: Each stressor was added during exponential growth (Figure 1A), causing an interruption to cell growth which caused a loss of polysomes by 15 min (Figure 1B, C), in accord with prior studies (Costello et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their growth curve experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 10 mM 3-AT treatment for 15 min caused an interruption to cell growth.
source: Each stressor was added during exponential growth (Figure 1A), causing an interruption to cell growth which caused a loss of polysomes by 15 min (Figure 1B, C), in accord with prior studies (Costello et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their growth curve experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: H2O2 and 3-AT treatment caused a loss of polysomes by 15 min.
source: Each stressor was added during exponential growth (Figure 1A), causing an interruption to cell growth which caused a loss of polysomes by 15 min (Figure 1B, C), in accord with prior studies (Costello et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their polysome profiling experiments shown in Figure 1B, C, and cites Costello et al., 2017.

claim: Growth recovered with time after stress treatment, showing that cells were able to adapt to each stressor.
source: Growth recovered with time, showing that the cells were able to adapt to each stressor (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their growth curve experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most proteins were restricted to the top of the sucrose gradient.
source: Qualitative analysis of protein migration through 15–50% sucrose gradients by sodium dodecyl sulphate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) indicated that most proteins were restricted to the top of the gradient, but that specific proteins did migrate deep into the gradient and were retained on polysomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Specific proteins migrated deep into the sucrose gradient and were retained on polysomes.
source: Qualitative analysis of protein migration through 15–50% sucrose gradients by sodium dodecyl sulphate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) indicated that most proteins were restricted to the top of the gradient, but that specific proteins did migrate deep into the gradient and were retained on polysomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from their SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Between 145 and 767 unique proteins were identified in at least two replicates of each gradient fraction.
source: Between 145 and 767 unique proteins were identified in at least two replicates of each gradient fraction (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1 – sheet 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was excellent correlation of the measured protein signal between replicates for unstressed fractions F1–F5 (r2 typically >0.9).
source: There was excellent correlation of the measured protein signal between replicates for unstressed fractions F1–F5 (r2 typically >0.9), but more divergence for stressed samples, especially in F4–F5 where, as expected from global polysome profiles, fewer proteins were found migrating deep into the sucrose gradients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was more divergence between replicates for stressed samples, especially in F4–F5.
source: There was excellent correlation of the measured protein signal between replicates for unstressed fractions F1–F5 (r2 typically >0.9), but more divergence for stressed samples, especially in F4–F5 where, as expected from global polysome profiles, fewer proteins were found migrating deep into the sucrose gradients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Fewer proteins were found migrating deep into the sucrose gradients in stressed samples.
source: There was excellent correlation of the measured protein signal between replicates for unstressed fractions F1–F5 (r2 typically >0.9), but more divergence for stressed samples, especially in F4–F5 where, as expected from global polysome profiles, fewer proteins were found migrating deep into the sucrose gradients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Principal component analysis showed good clustering of replicates for all three conditions.
source: Principal component analysis showed good clustering of replicates for all three conditions, with adjacent sucrose gradient fractions indicating a gradual change in their composition when moving in sequential order from monosomes (F1) to heavy polysomes (F5; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Adjacent sucrose gradient fractions showed a gradual change in their composition when moving from monosomes to heavy polysomes.
source: Principal component analysis showed good clustering of replicates for all three conditions, with adjacent sucrose gradient fractions indicating a gradual change in their composition when moving in sequential order from monosomes (F1) to heavy polysomes (F5; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 463 proteins were detected reproducibly in every fraction F1–F5 in unstressed conditions.
source: In unstressed conditions, 463 proteins were detected reproducibly in every fraction F1–F5, which rose to 516 when F5 was excluded (i.e. the same 516 proteins were identified in each fraction F1–F4; Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: 516 proteins were detected reproducibly in fractions F1–F4 in unstressed conditions.
source: In unstressed conditions, 463 proteins were detected reproducibly in every fraction F1–F5, which rose to 516 when F5 was excluded (i.e. the same 516 proteins were identified in each fraction F1–F4; Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: 353 proteins were identified in common in every fraction F1–F4 across all three conditions.
source: Nevertheless, 353 proteins were identified in common in every fraction F1–F4 across all three conditions (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: The 353 proteins found across F1–F4 in all conditions included 70 ribosomal proteins, 25 translation factors and regulatory proteins, 240 other known RBPs, and 18 proteins not previously designated as RNA- or ribosome-binding.
source: The proteins found across F1–F4 included 70 RPs, 25 TFs and regulatory proteins (TFs), 240 other known RBPs, as recently defined (Hentze et al., 2018), as well as 18 proteins that were not previously designated as RNA- or ribosome-binding (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1 – sheet 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2A, with RBP definitions from Hentze et al., 2018.

claim: A comparison of protein abundance in cytoplasmic extracts showed minimal change in LFQ intensity between stressed and control samples.
source: A comparison of protein abundance in cytoplasmic extracts showed minimal change in label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity (Tyanova et al., 2016) between stressed and control samples, indicating that the dramatic ribosome run-off within 15 min following stress did not have sufficient time to impact the total cellular protein content and that our method sampled cells during their adaptive phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The dramatic ribosome run-off within 15 min following stress did not have sufficient time to impact the total cellular protein content.
source: A comparison of protein abundance in cytoplasmic extracts showed minimal change in label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity (Tyanova et al., 2016) between stressed and control samples, indicating that the dramatic ribosome run-off within 15 min following stress did not have sufficient time to impact the total cellular protein content and that our method sampled cells during their adaptive phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the minimal change in protein abundance observed.

claim: The polysomal proteomics method sampled cells during their adaptive phase.
source: A comparison of protein abundance in cytoplasmic extracts showed minimal change in label-free quantification (LFQ) intensity (Tyanova et al., 2016) between stressed and control samples, indicating that the dramatic ribosome run-off within 15 min following stress did not have sufficient time to impact the total cellular protein content and that our method sampled cells during their adaptive phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the minimal change in protein abundance observed.

claim: There was no evidence that nascent protein chains or co-translational complex formation contributed significantly to the signal for polysome-associated proteins.
source: We also saw no evidence that either nascent protein chains or co-translational complex formation (Shiber et al., 2018) contributed significantly to the signal for our polysome-associated proteins.
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a conclusion from their analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cumulative amino- to carboxy-terminal peptide intensity profiles for individual proteins in total and ribosomal fractions showed no N-terminal bias in F1–F5 compared with T samples, except for rare examples.
source: Cumulative amino- to carboxy-terminal peptide intensity profiles for individual proteins in total and ribosomal fractions showed no N-terminal bias in F1–F5 compared with T samples, except for rare examples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, see Methods and figure legend for details).
evidence: The manuscript reports this as a result from their peptide intensity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ribosomal proteins and ribosome-associated chaperones were highly associated with ribosomes.
